final_proof:
**Conventions.** For a continuous $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ write $u=\operatorname{Re} f$, $v=\operatorname{Im} f$, so $f=u+iv$. The complex integral over a subinterval $[p,q]\subseteq[a,b]$ is defined by
$$\int_p^q f(t)\,dt=\int_p^q u(t)\,dt+i\int_p^q v(t)\,dt,$$
where the integrals on the right are real Riemann (Darboux) integrals. When $p=q$ the integral is $0$.

**Step 1 (the real and imaginary parts are integrable).** Since $|u(s)-u(t)|\le|f(s)-f(t)|$ and $|v(s)-v(t)|\le|f(s)-f(t)|$, the functions $u$ and $v$ are continuous real functions on $[a,b]$. So they are also continuous on every closed subinterval $[p,q]$ with $p<q$. A continuous real function on a closed bounded interval is Riemann integrable: it is uniformly continuous there, so any sufficiently fine partition makes its oscillation on each subinterval less than $\varepsilon/(q-p)$, which gives $U-L<\varepsilon$. So all the integrals below exist.

**Step 2 (real lemma).** Let $w:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and let $a<c<b$. Then $\int_a^c w+\int_c^b w=\int_a^b w$.

*Proof.* For a partition $P$, write $L(w,P)$ and $U(w,P)$ for its lower and upper Darboux sums. Let $P_1$ be any partition of $[a,c]$ and $P_2$ any partition of $[c,b]$. Then $P=P_1\cup P_2$ is a partition of $[a,b]$. Because $c$ is a point of both $P_1$ and $P_2$, the subintervals of $P$ are exactly the subintervals of $P_1$ together with those of $P_2$. A Darboux sum is a sum over subintervals, so
$$L(w,P)=L(w,P_1)+L(w,P_2),\qquad U(w,P)=U(w,P_1)+U(w,P_2).$$
Put $S=\int_a^c w+\int_c^b w$ and $I=\int_a^b w$. For any partition, the integral lies between the lower and upper sums. So $L(w,P_1)\le\int_a^c w\le U(w,P_1)$ and $L(w,P_2)\le\int_c^b w\le U(w,P_2)$. Adding these gives $L(w,P)\le S\le U(w,P)$. We also have $L(w,P)\le I\le U(w,P)$. Since $S$ and $I$ both lie in $[L(w,P),U(w,P)]$,
$$|S-I|\le U(w,P)-L(w,P)=\big(U(w,P_1)-L(w,P_1)\big)+\big(U(w,P_2)-L(w,P_2)\big).$$
Let $\varepsilon>0$. By Step 1, $w$ is integrable on $[a,c]$ and on $[c,b]$, so we can choose $P_1$ and $P_2$ with $U(w,P_j)-L(w,P_j)<\varepsilon/2$ for $j=1,2$. Then $|S-I|<\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $S=I$. $\square$

**Step 3 (the complex statement).** Let $c\in[a,b]$.

*Case $c=a$.* Then $\int_a^c f=\int_a^a f=0$ and $\int_c^b f=\int_a^b f$, so the identity holds.

*Case $c=b$.* Then $\int_c^b f=\int_b^b f=0$ and $\int_a^c f=\int_a^b f$, so the identity holds.

These two cases also cover $a=b$.

*Case $a<c<b$.* Apply Step 2 with $w=u$ and with $w=v$:
$$\int_a^c u+\int_c^b u=\int_a^b u,\qquad \int_a^c v+\int_c^b v=\int_a^b v.$$
By the definition of the complex integral,
$$\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f=\Big(\int_a^c u+i\int_a^c v\Big)+\Big(\int_c^b u+i\int_c^b v\Big)=\Big(\int_a^c u+\int_c^b u\Big)+i\Big(\int_a^c v+\int_c^b v\Big)=\int_a^b u+i\int_a^b v=\int_a^b f.$$

So in every case
$$\int_a^c f(t)\,dt+\int_c^b f(t)\,dt=\int_a^b f(t)\,dt. \qquad\blacksquare$$
